what_it_does: Standard neural networks multiply weight numbers by input numbers billions of times per inference; multipliers are expensive in silicon area and power. AdderNet replaces those multiplications with a cheaper operation: computing the sum of absolute differences (SAD) — essentially measuring how far apart two numbers are rather than multiplying them — which can be done with simple adder circuits instead of multiplier circuits. The challenge addressed here is that making AdderNet weights use very few bits (a technique called quantization — representing numbers with cruder, smaller values to save memory and speed up computation) is harder for SAD than for standard multiply-based networks. NN-AdderNet forces the weights to be non-negative (no negative values), which means the sign bit — one of the bits in each stored number — is always zero and can be dropped, saving one bit per weight for free. The remaining weights also tend to be mostly zero (sparse), so the paper adds a compression step that skips storing those zeros, further shrinking the model. Together these two tricks make AdderNet models significantly smaller and cheaper to deploy on low-power hardware.
